title: Strategy: swap how it works
summary: Hold a job behind an interface, so a different class can be swapped in without changing the code that uses it.

say.never: A maps app can plan your trip by car, by bike or on foot. The app doesn't have three copies of its code. It holds one **strategy** for working out the route, and you swap which one it uses. In Java, the strategy is an interface, each way of doing the job is a class that implements it, and the code that uses it only ever talks to the interface.
say.bit: **Strategy**: an interface for the job, one class per way of doing it, and code that only knows the interface.

steps.title: In your lesson: One job, many ways

say.never: `DriveMode` is the job: turn a `Gamepad` reading into `WheelSpeeds`. `TankDrive` and `ArcadeDrive` are two ways of doing it. Each one needs `implements DriveMode`, a `getName()`, and a `calculate(Gamepad pad)` that builds a `new WheelSpeeds(left, right)`. For arcade, work out both sides, then keep each one between `-1.0` and `1.0` with `Math.max` and `Math.min`.
say.bit: `TankDrive` and `ArcadeDrive` implement `DriveMode`: `getName()` and `calculate(pad)`. Arcade clamps each side.

say.never: The code that *uses* a strategy keeps it in a field whose type is the interface, not a class. Then any strategy fits in that field, and a setter can swap it while the program runs. The method that does the work just calls the interface's method. It never asks "which one are you?", so a brand-new strategy written next year works without changing a line.
say.bit: Keep the strategy in a field of the interface type, swap it with a setter, and just call its method.

steps.title: In your lesson: Hold it by its interface

say.never: `Drivetrain` keeps its strategy in `mode_`. The constructor and `setMode` fill it in (but `setMode(null)` leaves it alone). `getModeName()` and `drive(pad)` just ask `mode_`. No `instanceof`, no `if` on the name.
